canonical_statement: The VITAL trial evaluated whether total intravenous anesthesia with propofol, compared with volatile inhalational anesthesia, improves days alive and at home at 30 days and other patient-centered outcomes after major noncardiac surgery.

VITAL was a pragmatic, multicenter, open-label randomized clinical trial conducted at 49 UK National Health Service hospitals from January 2022 through April 2024, with final follow-up in October 2024.
Participants were eligible if they were aged 50 years or older and scheduled for elective major noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia.

population.label: Randomized adults aged 50 years or older undergoing elective major noncardiac surgery at 49 UK NHS hospitals
inclusion_criteria: Elective major noncardiac surgery under general anesthesia

canonical_statement: Patients were excluded if either anesthetic technique was contraindicated or if they were not expected to survive 30 days.

population.label: Patients screened for VITAL
exclusion_criteria: Contraindication to either total intravenous anesthesia or volatile inhalational anesthesia

canonical_statement: Participants were randomized 1:1 on the day of surgery using computerized minimization balanced for surgical specialty, expected surgical duration, cancer status, and Rockwood frailty category.
Treating clinicians were not blinded to allocation, while patients were not explicitly informed of their randomized anesthetic technique.
The TIVA arm used propofol as the intended primary anesthetic maintenance technique, without a protocol-mandated dose threshold.

concept.text: Total intravenous anesthesia (TIVA) using propofol as the intended primary maintenance technique

canonical_statement: The comparator arm used a volatile inhalational anesthetic as the intended primary anesthetic maintenance technique.

concept.text: Volatile inhalational anesthesia as the intended primary maintenance technique

canonical_statement: Perioperative care other than the randomized maintenance anesthetic technique was left to clinician discretion.
The primary outcome was days alive and at home within 30 days after surgery; days spent in hospital counted as zero home days, and death within 30 days resulted in a score of zero.

concept.text: Days alive and at home at 30 days

outcome.definition: Number of days from surgery through day 30 spent alive and outside hospital; death within 30 days assigned 0 days.

canonical_statement: Prespecified secondary outcomes included days alive and at home at 90 days, mortality at 30 days, 90 days, and 6 months, quality of recovery, patient satisfaction, delirium, awareness, and major postoperative complications.

concept.text: Prespecified secondary clinical and patient-reported outcomes

canonical_statement: The planned sample size was 2500 participants, providing 90% power at a 2-sided alpha of .05 to detect a 1-day difference in days alive and at home at 30 days under an assumed mean of 25 days and SD of 7.5 days.

The primary intention-to-treat analysis used zero-inflated negative binomial regression adjusted for the randomization stratification variables and included participants with available primary-outcome data.
Secondary outcome analyses were not adjusted for multiple comparisons.
The trial prespecified a per-protocol primary-outcome analysis and subgroup analyses based on stratification variables and prior hospital use of TIVA.
A total of 2508 participants were randomized, with 1254 assigned to TIVA and 1254 assigned to inhalational anesthesia.

canonical_statement: The prespecified 90-day mortality noninferiority objective was underpowered because observed overall 90-day mortality was substantially lower than assumed; the supplement states the achieved sample could not exclude the planned relative-risk increases of 1.5 or 1.6.
The investigators reported no apparent differences in prespecified subgroup analyses of primary and secondary outcomes.

The investigators concluded that TIVA did not improve days alive and at home at 30 days compared with inhalational anesthesia in adults aged 50 years or older undergoing elective major noncardiac surgery.
The investigators concluded that exploratory improvements in early postoperative comfort with TIVA did not translate into differences in complication rates or longer-term recovery.
The trial was unblinded, which could affect subjective patient-reported outcomes, although patients were not explicitly informed of allocation.
The definition of home included any location outside an acute hospital, so rehabilitation and discharge pathways could influence the days-alive-and-at-home outcome.
The trial did not evaluate long-term oncological outcomes.
The low incidence of unintentional awareness prevented definitive comparative safety conclusions for awareness.
Because all sites were in the UK National Health Service, findings may not generalize to health systems with different perioperative practices or patient populations.

The trial enrolled elective-surgery patients who were predominantly well by the Rockwood frailty scale and predominantly underwent intra-abdominal surgery, limiting applicability to emergency, frail, cognitively impaired, and urgent-surgery populations.
Regional anesthesia use was high in both groups (78.2% with TIVA and 78.3% with inhalational anesthesia), which may limit generalizability to settings with different regional-anesthesia practice.
The study did not establish the cost-effectiveness of TIVA; further economic evaluation related to recovery pathways and resource utilization was identified as needed.
